summary: Technical workshop focused on on-prem air-gapped deployment logistics and performance tuning for Ironwood's inference cluster. Main topics: artifact delivery and signing, offline license activation, GPU driver compatibility, KV cache warmup strategies, batching/latency tradeoffs, quantization impact on throughput and accuracy. Agreed pilot nodes and next steps for checklist and benchmarks.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-20 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~58m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Tom Liao (Ironwood Infra Lead), Aisha Patel (Ironwood ML Eng), Rand O'Neal (Ironwood CTO)

[00:00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. quick agenda from our side — we want to walk through the artifact delivery plan for air-gapped installs, cover offline licensing, and then dig into runtime perf: kv cache warmup, batching, and quant quantization tradeoffs.

[00:00:18] Tom: sounds good. we've had a couple internal debates about handing usb drives to field engineers vs sealed HSM transfer. security's leaning sealed, but ops wants speed.

[00:00:30] Maya: totally. we'll show the signed bundle approach — GPG + SHA256 + manifest — that our ops team uses. Diego i think you had a slide or a quick runbook?

[00:00:40] Diego: yep, i pulled a lightweight runbook. main points: artifact bundle is S3 -> airgap export -> sign with our offline signing key, put the signature and manifest together in a tar.gz, then provide the bundle to customer via encrypted usb or physical media. we recommend a chain of custody doc. note, some customers want PGP, some want their own signing authority.

[00:01:10] Aisha: quick q — what does the footprint look like on the usb? model files, runtime libs, driver packages? how big are we talking for a 13B quantized model?

[00:01:22] Diego: for 13B quant int8-ish builds you're looking 6–12GB compressed for model shards, runtime + small libs ~2GB, driver packages depend on cuda/cuDNN versions — those can be big. overall safe to assume 32GB stick per node to be comfortable.

[00:01:40] Tom: and encryption during transit? we want both encryption-at-rest for the stick and a tamper-evident seal.

[00:01:47] Maya: yes recommend full disk encryption on USB and a tamper-evident hash on packaging. our runbook has a hash-check step and an rpc to our licensing server for activation once media is loaded. in air-gapped mode, activation is done with offline license tokens — Diego?

[00:02:05] Diego: right. offline licensing: we generate an activation blob tied to customer HW IDs (or cluster cert) and an expiry/policy. customer runs the activation script which validates manifest signature, then applies license to node. we provide both an interactive and fully automated appliance script.

[00:02:30] Rand: is that tied to MACs or xen/VM identifiers? we can't have ephemeral ids break license activation in our k8s cluster.

[00:02:38] Diego: we prefer stable hardware identifiers — TPM or platform UUID. we also support cluster-level licensing where the license is bound to a cluster cert you create once. that avoids problems with VM churn.

[00:03:00] Aisha: moving to drivers — we've had inconsistent perf between H100 and A100. what are the recommended driver/cuda combos and any mitigations for kernel incompat?

[00:03:10] Diego: good one. H100: CUDA 12.x + cuDNN 9.x in our tests; A100: CUDA 11.8 + cuDNN 8.x tends to be stable. but there's overlap; sometimes 12 supports A100 with specific driver builds. we ship a compatibility matrix — i'll send current matrix. two things — for H100 MIG-like configs and MPS settings can change perf; second, kernel modules need to be certed for our runtime (we validate certain nvidia driver versions).

[00:03:45] Tom: do you require specific firmware on the cards? we've held off on firmware updates in prod.

[00:03:50] Diego: we list recommended firmware versions; it's not always mandatory but there are perf and stability fixes in newer firmwares. we advise staged upgrades in pilot.

[00:04:10] Maya: okay shifting to runtime perf: Aisha mentioned cold-starts. Diego, can you explain KV cache warmup strategies and approximate warmup times for a 1k prefix distribution?

[00:04:22] Diego: sure. two axes: KV cache priming (loading cached keys/values) and model cold-start JITs (if any). for our runtime, KV warmup depends on how many unique prefixes you expect. if your workload has long conversation prefixes, warmup can cost 50–200ms per prefix per shard on first token generation, but subsequent tokens hit the KV cache and are much faster. for a 13B model with optimized kernels on A100, we'd see median token latency drop from ~220ms cold to ~30–40ms warm under single-request scenarios. batching changes that of course.

[00:05:00] Aisha: those numbers match what we saw but our tail spikes to 800ms at times during bursts.

[00:05:05] Diego: tail spikes often come from synchronous disk access during model shard load or from insufficient prefetch. in air-gapped installs we recommend an initial prefetch step as part of node provisioning that reads model shards into RAM/disk cache and runs a small synthetic workload to prime kernels. we provide a warmup script that mimics your request distribution.

[00:05:30] Tom: question about KV eviction — when memory pressure is high, what's the policy? LRU? TTL?

[00:05:37] Diego: default is LRU with configurable per-tenant quotas. you can also set TTL-based eviction for conversational workloads where old prefixes are less useful. tuning depends on working set size. we can provide telemetry hooks to tell you hit rates.

[00:05:55] Rand: on batching — we want predictable 95th percentile latency under 100ms for interactive use. how do batching parameters interact with that SLO?

[00:06:05] Diego: batching is a tradeoff: higher batch windows increase throughput and reduce cost per token but inflate latency. our adaptive batching can be configured with max_batch_wait (ms) and target batch size. with 100ms p95 target, we'd set max_batch_wait ~15–30ms and target batch size small (2–8) depending on request arrival rate. also continuous batching vs windowed batching differ; continuous batching has lower average latency but can create more tail variance.

[00:06:35] Aisha: what about dynamic batching for mixed-length prompts? long prompts blocking short ones is a concern.

[00:06:42] Diego: we use length-aware batching — the scheduler groups similar sequence-length requests to avoid head-of-line blocking. we also allow priority tagging so interactive (low-latency) requests skip large long-running batches. that's part of the request metadata you can send.

[00:06:58] Maya: quantization — Aisha, you mentioned quality concerns with int8 for your LLM. Diego, what's the real-world throughput/quality win vs int16 or fp16?

[00:07:08] Diego: int8 quant gives 1.8–2.5x throughput uplift on GPUs with quant-friendly kernels and lower memory footprint enabling larger batch sizes. quality can drop for certain instruction-heavy prompts — often ~0.5–2% eval delta on our rouge/accuracy tests but it's model dependent. we recommend running the Redwood Optimize eval harness on a representative prompt set before switching. we also have mixed-precision pathways (fp16 storage + int8 compute) for better quality/throughput balance.

[00:07:40] Aisha: can we do per-route quantization? some routes are more tolerant of quant vs others.

[00:07:44] Diego: yes — per-route model variants are supported. you can pin routes to a high-quality fp16 model and route less-critical endpoints to quantized variants. routing can be policy-driven — cost vs latency thresholds.

[00:07:57] Tom: offline diagnostics — if we see weird perf regressions, what debug artifacts do you need?

[00:08:05] Diego: ideally: kernel logs, runtime trace for that request, model shard checksums, driver versions, and a small failing prompt. we have automated trace collectors that can run in air-gapped mode and bundle traces with a signed envelope for us to analyze.

[00:08:25] Rand: what about fallback policies in case a node loses license or runs out of capacity? we need graceful degradation not hard failure.

[00:08:34] Maya: we support automatic fallback to a hosted variant (if allowed) or to a smaller model variant locally. in pure air-gapped customers, we support multi-tier local variants and can return a 503 with metadata to signal a soft-fail.

[00:08:50] Aisha: curious about metrics — can we get per-prefix latency histograms and token-level cost?

[00:08:58] Diego: yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level breakdowns, and for Private we ship an agent that aggregates per-route and per-prefix metrics. in air-gapped mode the agent writes metrics to a local Prometheus endpoint and you can choose how often to scrape or export.

[00:09:15] Tom: any gotchas with k8s local PV for model shards? we worry about eviction and cold reboots.

[00:09:22] Diego: use node-local SSDs where possible or a local PV with high reclaim policies; networked mounts increase jitter. we also recommend a small pre-stage script to ensure shards are present on boot.

[00:09:40] Maya: going back to warmup — Diego mentioned synthetic workload. what's the script look like? does it need real keys?

[00:09:47] Diego: synthetic workload hits typical prefixes you provide. it can use anonymized prompt sets — no real data required. it does: sequential token generation to prime KV, a few batch runs to warm kernels, and perf samplings. script outputs a warmup report with hit rates and median latencies.

[00:10:08] Aisha: ok, practical — we want to schedule a 3-node pilot next month. what's a minimal hardware spec for the pilot to be representative?

[00:10:16] Diego: recommended pilot: 3 x 80GB GPU nodes (A100 or H100 depending on availability), 256GB RAM, 2 x 2TB NVMe for model shards + OS. that's close to prod-like. if you want to save cost, 2 x A100 + 1 x H100 mix is workable but results vary.

[00:10:38] Tom: timeline for bundle delivery? we need to sync with our procurement for physical transfer.

[00:10:44] Maya: once we get cluster certs and license details, Redwood can produce signed bundles within 3 business days. driver checklist and compatibility matrix we can send today.

[00:10:55] Rand: about audit and compliance — we need audit logs for license activation and artifact install. do you provide tamper-evident logs?

[00:11:03] Diego: audit logs are part of Private. activation events, signature verification, and install steps are logged locally and can be exported as signed attestation files.

[00:11:15] Aisha: small note — sometimes transcription engines turn KV into K V cash in our logs. just a laugh.

[00:11:20] (laughter)

[00:11:28] Maya: next block let's look at a live config snippet and a proposed rollout plan — diego you want to share screen?

[00:11:35] Diego: sure. i'm pasting a sample config (spoken):
- runtime.kv_cache.size: 64GB per-gpu
- runtime.batcher.max_wait_ms: 20
- runtime.batcher.target_size: 8
- model.variant.fp16: /opt/redwood/models/13b-fp16
- model.variant.int8: /opt/redwood/models/13b-int8
- license.mode: cluster_cert

[00:12:05] Diego: notes: set kv_cache to fraction of GPU memory + app working set. for heavy conversational you might go 80GB, for stateless short prompts smaller.

[00:12:20] Tom: great. can you also include the exact commands to verify driver module signatures and gst logs? team needs the commands for the runbook.

[00:12:29] Diego: yes i'll add commands: nvidia-smi -a, modinfo nvidia, sha256sum on driver rpm, and our redwood-verify.sh which checks manifest+signature.

[00:12:40] Maya: we've seen customers want SLA grammar in offline mode — do you support any uptime commitments for private/on-prem installs?

[00:12:46] Diego: enterprise support tiers include response SLAs and runbook help; however uptime SLAs with financial penalties are typically for Dedicated/reserved contracts where we control infra. for private on-prem we offer a support add-on with guaranteed response times.

[00:13:05] Aisha: one more on quantization workflows — can we A/B test quantized variants automatically?

[00:13:10] Diego: yes — rollout policies support canary and A/B routing plus automatic rollback on regression thresholds. Redwood Optimize can automatically run evals and tie regressions to releases.

[00:13:20] Tom: good. let's talk about diagnostics during pilot: can we run token-level sampling at 1% of traffic to keep overhead low?

[00:13:27] Diego: you can. sampling plus local aggregation works well; we'd suggest 1–2% to start.

[00:13:35] Maya: quick recap action items before we run out of time. diego will send driver/compat matrix and warmup script, maya to send pricing and license runbook, tom to confirm transfer SOP and target pilot nodes. agreed?

[00:13:48] Tom: yes. i'll get procurement involved and aim to confirm by 2025-12-24.

[00:13:55] Rand: one last — any hidden dependencies we should be aware of at OS level? glibc versions?

[00:14:01] Diego: we test against RHEL 8.x and Ubuntu 22.04 primarily; some runtime libs need glibc >= 2.31. we'll include exact distro+kernel recommendations.

[00:14:12] Maya: perfect. thanks all. will record these notes. we'll follow up with the artifacts and proposed dates.

[00:14:20] (end of recorded segment, remaining time used for offline q&a and side chat)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings (KV cache -> "K V cash","quantization" -> "quant quant") present; speaker labels partially inferred.
